title: Advanced Leadership
tagline: Move from leading a team to leading leaders, functions and change, with judgement, influence and integrity.
description:
Most managers are promoted for being good at the work. The step to senior leadership asks for something different: you now lead people who lead others, you decide with incomplete information, you need support from colleagues you do not control, and the culture of your function starts to look like you.

**Advanced Leadership** is built for that step. Over five sessions you will work on how you lead yourself under pressure, how you think and decide strategically, how you build teams of managers who own results, how you lead change and win support without formal authority, and how you set a culture that performs ethically and lasts beyond you.

Every idea is applied to realistic situations from Pakistani organisations: a bank rolling out a new core system, a telecom restructuring its regions, an FMCG business entering new cities, a family-owned group professionalising its management. Each session ends with a scored test, and the certification closes with a demanding, timed final exam built on scenarios where more than one answer looks reasonable. Passing it shows that you can apply senior leadership judgement, not just recall theory.
audience: Mid-level and senior managers who already lead teams and now lead other managers or a whole function
Newly promoted heads of department, regional heads and general managers
High-potential leaders in succession pools preparing for wider responsibility
Project and transformation leads who must drive change across functions they do not control
Founders and family members professionalising the management of a growing business
outcomes: Lead yourself deliberately: know your values and triggers, regulate emotion under pressure and show steady executive presence
Frame strategic problems, choose the right decision approach for the level of uncertainty and guard against common biases
Build teams of managers with real trust and accountability, delegate at scale and coach leaders to grow
Plan and lead change by mapping stakeholders, building coalitions and working with resistance rather than against it
Influence peers, seniors and partners without relying on positional authority
Shape an ethical, high-performing culture, handle difficult conversations well and build resilience and succession

quest.name: The Karakoram Ascent
quest.premise: You have just been promoted to head the Northern Division of a Lahore-based consumer goods group, and the Group CEO wants it to lead the company's next climb. Your coach, a retired high-altitude climber, calls it the Karakoram Ascent. The mountain will not reward strength alone: the higher you climb, the more you depend on judgement, on rope teams that trust each other, and on people you cannot order about. From Base Camp to the Summit Ridge, each stage tests a different side of senior leadership. Reach the top, pass the final ascent, and earn your place among those who lead leaders.

badge.name: Summit Leader
badge.description: Awarded for completing The Karakoram Ascent and passing the Advanced Leadership final exam: proven judgement in leading leaders, change and culture.

cast.name: Nasreen Baig

cast.name: Sana Baloch

cast.name: Faraz Akhtar

sessions.title: Leading Yourself: Identity, Values and Presence
sessions.summary: Before you lead leaders, you lead yourself. Redefine what your job now is, clarify the values you lead by, manage your emotions and triggers under pressure, see your blind spots and build an executive presence based on substance.
objectives: Explain how the job changes when you move from leading a team to leading leaders or a function
Turn personal values into clear operating principles and use them in hard trade-offs
Apply the four areas of emotional intelligence to manage triggers and pressure
Use structured feedback to uncover blind spots that grow with seniority
Show executive presence through composure, clarity and concise communication

cards.title: Day 31: The queue outside your door
cards.setting: Your new corner office, Northern Division headquarters, Gulberg, Lahore. 8:40 p.m.

lines.text: Thirty-one days ago you were promoted to head the Northern Division of a Lahore-based consumer goods group: five regional managers, two plants, 1,900 people. Tonight your desk is buried.
Sorry to catch you this late. Fourteen distributor credit exceptions are still waiting for your signature. Two distributors in Chakwal stopped ordering today because of it.
Sana was your fellow regional manager for eight years. Now she reports to you, and she is too polite to say what she is thinking. Your phone lights up with a WhatsApp.
Your three-year division plan was due on Monday. The board meets in ten days. What exactly is taking so long?
You were the best regional manager this group had. So you still check route plans, sign every exception and visit outlets to fix displays yourself. You have not written one page of the plan.
May I tell you what the mountains taught me? On the approach to K2, the climber who insists on carrying every load collapses before Camp I. The leader carries something else.
Every expedition starts at Base Camp, in what I call the Mirror Tent. Before you lead anyone up this mountain, you lead yourself. So, tonight's question: what is your job now?

cards.title: The three shifts of leading leaders

scenes.heading: Same mountain, new job
scenes.narration: Every step up the ladder changes three things at once: the skills you need, how you spend your time, and what you value about work. Most leaders who stumble are not weak. They are still doing the job one level down.

scenes.heading: Shift one: your time
scenes.narration: Your hours now belong to three things: setting direction, building the managers below you, and working with peers across the business. Checking route plans is no longer one of them.

scenes.heading: Shift two: what you value
scenes.narration: This is the hardest shift. Your output is no longer the files you touch. It is the capability of your managers. Fix a problem yourself and you solve one. Build a manager who can fix it and you solve the next hundred.

scenes.heading: Shift three: functions you never ran
scenes.narration: Lead several functions and you must learn and value the ones you never worked in, and balance your attention across all of them, instead of living in your old favourite.

scenes.heading: Three warning signs
scenes.narration: Watch for three signs. Decisions queue at your desk. You skip levels by habit and fix things yourself. And your calendar still looks like your old job.

cards.title: What changes when you lead leaders
cards.caption: Your real output is now other people's capability. If your week looks like the left column, you have not yet made the move.

items.label: Problems
items.right: Building managers who solve them

items.label: Measured on
items.right: A system of teams and its results

items.label: Expertise
items.right: Balancing functions you never ran

items.label: Horizon
items.right: Quarters and years

items.label: What you value
items.right: Other people's success

cards.title: Audit your calendar
cards.prompt: These are real items from your first month. Sort each one: is it your job now, or work your managers should own?

items.text: Setting the division's three-year direction
Approving routine distributor credit exceptions
Coaching a regional manager after a tough quarter
Rewriting a sales officer's weekly route plan
Building a joint plan with the heads of supply and finance
Resolving an individual staff payroll query
Deciding which decision types each manager will own
Visiting an outlet alone to fix its shelf display

cards.question: Three months into the role, which sign most clearly shows you have NOT yet made the shift to leading leaders?
options: You spend two half-days a week on planning and peer meetings
You visit branches together with the area manager and coach them afterwards
Your managers hold decisions until you have looked at them
You review a monthly sample of exceptions rather than every file
cards.explanation: When managers wait for you instead of deciding, you have become the bottleneck and are still doing the old job. The other three are signs of a healthy transition: protected time for direction, coaching alongside managers, and sampling rather than approving everything.

cards.title: Turn values into operating principles
cards.prompt: Nasreen hands you a blank card. 'Integrity on a poster tells nobody what to do.' Put her five steps for building operating principles in order.
steps: Recall your proudest and your lowest leadership moments; your values hide in those stories
Name three to five core values, because a long list cannot guide a choice
Write each value as a specific behaviour, e.g. 'I decide promotions on evidence I could show the people not chosen'
Test each principle against a real dilemma; if it would not change your decision, it is too vague
Share the principles with your team so they can predict your decisions and act without asking

cards.question: Your principle is 'I appoint distributors on criteria I could publish.' A board member calls to recommend his brother-in-law for the new Abbottabad distributorship. What is most consistent with your principle?
options: Put him on the shortlist as a courtesy, then let the panel decide
Tell the board member he is welcome to apply and will be judged on the same published criteria
Adopt a new rule that relatives of board members cannot apply
Quietly pass the file to procurement without mentioning the call
cards.explanation: A principle only protects you if it applies the same way whoever is asking, and you say so openly. A courtesy shortlist bends the criteria. A blanket ban is a different rule you never adopted and is unfair to the applicant. Passing the file quietly avoids the issue without transparency. When values collide, such as loyalty versus fairness, decide which takes priority and explain why.

cards.title: The review that went wrong
cards.setting: Monthly divisional review, conference room, 10 a.m. Twelve managers around the table.

lines.text: At 8 a.m., Javed called you about stock-outs in Murree. 'Is this how you run a division?' You walk into your review two hours later with your jaw tight.
On the Murree stock-outs: our transport vendor lost two trucks to the landslide on the expressway, and the backup vendor needs a week's notice. I want to explain the risk for next month as well.
Heat rises in your face. Before you can think, the words are out: 'I don't want stories, Sana. I want results.' The room goes silent. Nobody raises a single risk for the rest of the meeting.
That was a hijack. Your brain's alarm fired before your reasoning caught up. You felt exposed by Javed this morning, and Sana paid for it.
Notice what the room learned: bad news gets punished here. The landslide risk was exactly what you needed to hear. Now the question is not whether you were wrong. It is how you repair it.

cards.title: Emotional intelligence builds from the base
cards.caption: Read from the bottom up. Self-awareness is the foundation: you cannot manage an emotion you have not noticed, and you cannot read others while flooded by your own.

items.label: Relationship management
items.detail: Outward: acting on what you read. Influencing, resolving conflict, coaching, building networks.

items.label: Social awareness
items.detail: Outward: reading the room, unspoken concerns and the dynamics of a group.

items.label: Self-management
items.detail: Inward: staying composed and choosing your response instead of acting on impulse.

items.label: Self-awareness
items.detail: Inward: knowing your moods, triggers, strengths and limits as they happen.

cards.back: Under threat, the brain's fast alarm triggers fight or flight before the reasoning part catches up. A public challenge can provoke words you regret within seconds.

cards.front: Your best defence in the moment
cards.back: Create a gap between trigger and response: a slow breath, a clarifying question ('Help me understand your concern'), or an agreed pause ('Let me come back to you by tomorrow').
Holding the emotion in, then letting it out later or elsewhere, such as staying calm in the meeting and sending your managers a harsh blame email at midnight.
Noticing the emotion, naming it and choosing your response, then dealing with the issue at a time and place you pick.

cards.front: Why your mood matters more now
cards.back: A senior leader's emotion spreads. People adjust, hide bad news and tell you what you want to hear. Leaders are often the last to know their mood is setting the tone.
Neither. Counter-attacking escalates the hijack. Going silent or falsely agreeing is suppression. Pause, clarify, then answer on the facts.

cards.title: Repairing the damage
cards.situation: It is the evening after the review. You know you shut Sana down in front of twelve colleagues, and that everyone learned that raising a risk gets punished. The next review is in four weeks. What do you do?

choices.text: Apologise to Sana privately tomorrow, then tell the whole group at the next review that you shut down important information, and open every review with a 'risks and blockers' slot
choices.outcome: Sana walks you through the vendor risk in detail. At the next review, the room relaxes when you own the mistake, and the new risks slot brings three issues to light weeks earlier than usual. The repair was as visible as the damage, and the routine change shows it will not happen again.

choices.text: Apologise to Sana privately and sincerely, and leave it there
choices.outcome: Sana appreciates it, and your relationship recovers. But the other eleven managers never hear it. Their lesson, 'bad news gets punished', stays in place, and risks keep arriving late. A private apology cannot fix a public lesson.

choices.text: Apologise at the next review, but explain that the CEO had put you under heavy pressure that morning
choices.outcome: The 'but' cancels the apology. People hear an excuse, not ownership, and conclude that your temper depends on Javed's mood. Nobody volunteers a risk.

choices.text: Say nothing. You were under pressure, and people will forget by next month
choices.outcome: They do not forget. Over the next quarter, problems surface only when they become crises, and you start hearing about issues from Javed before your own team. Silence fixed nothing.

cards.title: Keep a trigger log for two weeks
cards.body:
For two working weeks, note every strong negative reaction at work: **what happened**, **what you felt** (name it precisely: embarrassed, disrespected, anxious), **what you did** and **what you wish you had done**.

Most leaders find two or three repeating patterns, such as being questioned in front of seniors. For each one, **plan a default response in advance**, for example: acknowledge the question, then ask what concerns them most. A planned response is far easier to use under pressure than willpower, and far better than trying to predict every possible question.

cards.question: In a budget meeting you notice that the head of marketing goes quiet and glances at Faraz whenever cuts are mentioned. Which of these would be relationship management rather than social awareness?
options: Noticing the glances and sensing an unspoken disagreement
Feeling your own irritation rise as the meeting drags on
Inviting both of them to talk it through after the meeting so the tension is resolved
Realising you tend to get defensive when budgets are cut
cards.explanation: Social awareness is noticing and reading others, as in the first option. Relationship management is acting on what you read, such as bringing the two together to resolve the tension. The second and fourth options are about your own emotions, which is self-awareness.

cards.title: The Mirror Tent
cards.setting: A quiet room at a hotel in Islamabad. Nasreen has your 360-degree feedback report.

lines.text: Your peers rate you highly on 'listens before deciding'. Your own managers rate you low. Same person, two pictures.
You frown. Every week you ask your managers, 'Any feedback for me?' Every week they say, 'No, all good.'
Can I be honest, as someone who sat beside you for eight years? People soften things for you now. You control their bonuses. 'All good' is the safe answer.
In my old company we never told the boss anything. You do not correct a senior in public. We talked about it in the canteen instead.
Power filters what reaches you. The higher you climb, the bigger your blind spot grows, unless you work to shrink it. So what will you do with this report?

cards.title: The Johari window
cards.caption: Grow the open pane. Feedback shrinks the blind pane; appropriate self-disclosure shrinks the hidden one. With seniority the blind pane tends to grow, because power filters candid feedback.

axes.x: Known to you → not known to you

items.label: Open
items.detail: Known to you and to others. The bigger this pane, the more people trust and predict you.

items.label: Blind
items.detail: Others see it; you do not. Shrink it by asking for specific feedback and rewarding honesty.

items.label: Hidden
items.detail: You know it; others do not. Shrink it through appropriate self-disclosure.

items.label: Unknown
items.detail: Known to nobody yet. New challenges sometimes bring it to light.

cards.title: Feedback moves that work
cards.prompt: Match each situation to the move that gets you honest feedback.

pairs.left: 'Any feedback for me?' always gets 'All good'
pairs.right: Ask one specific, forward-looking question, e.g. 'What one thing would make our reviews more useful?'

pairs.left: Someone gives you your first candid comment
pairs.right: Thank them, do not defend, and act visibly; it decides whether a second comment ever comes

pairs.left: Your 360 shows your team rates your listening low
pairs.right: Thank the team, share the theme, commit to one specific change and ask for check-ins

pairs.left: You are new to Islamic finance and your team knows more
pairs.right: Say so openly: self-disclosure enlarges your open area by shrinking the hidden one

pairs.left: You need someone who will say what others will not
pairs.right: Find a truth-teller, such as a peer or mentor outside your reporting line

cards.question: Which response to your 360 report is most likely to protect your blind spot and reduce future feedback?
options: Committing to one visible change and asking for monthly check-ins
Debriefing the report with a coach before reacting
Asking HR which managers gave you the low scores so you can understand them
Sharing the main theme with your team and thanking them
cards.explanation: Trying to identify who wrote the comments breaks anonymity and tells everyone that honesty is risky, so future feedback dries up. The other three reward honesty: a coach helps you absorb it calmly, and sharing the theme plus a visible change shows people that feedback leads to action.

cards.title: Executive presence: substance, shown well
cards.body:
Presence is what makes senior people trust your judgement. It is not polish or a loud voice. It rests on three pillars:

- **Composure:** steady when things go wrong. In a crisis, people watch your face before they hear your words. Open with **what we know, what we do not know yet, and what happens next**, not speculation, blame or promises you cannot keep.
- **Clarity:** your view and your ask in a few sentences.
- **Credibility:** you know the numbers, admit what you do not know and do what you said.

**In hierarchical rooms**, presence means stating your view respectfully but unambiguously, holding it calmly with evidence when pushed, and changing it **only for a better argument, not for seniority**. Changing your mind when someone brings better data builds credibility; clinging to a disproven view destroys it.

cards.title: Brief like a senior
cards.caption: Never tell the story in the order it happened. Senior listeners may interrupt before you reach the point.

items.label: Bottom line
items.detail: The conclusion or decision you need, in one sentence: 'I recommend we pause the launch for four weeks.'

items.label: Why
items.detail: Two or three reasons, each with one key number.

items.label: What next
items.detail: Risks, what you need from them, and by when. Offer detail only if asked.

cards.title: The boardroom push-back
cards.situation: At the board meeting you recommend delaying a new Quetta depot until a transport-cost audit is finished. A senior director cuts in: 'We did not hire you to be cautious. Approve it.' Javed looks at you. You believe the cost data is incomplete.

choices.text: Restate the recommendation calmly with the two key numbers, and say you will change your view if new evidence shows the costs are sound
choices.outcome: The room settles. Faraz asks a sharp follow-up that supports your point, and the board agrees to a six-week delay. Afterwards, the director tells Javed you 'hold your ground without making it personal'. That is presence.

choices.text: Withdraw the recommendation; contradicting a senior director in front of the board is unwise
choices.outcome: The depot is approved without the audit. Three months later, transport costs run 80% over plan. The board now wonders why you did not say more, and your silence costs you credibility.

choices.text: Ask the chair to defer the item so you can bring the full audit next month
choices.outcome: Reasonable if the uncertainty were genuine, but you already hold strong evidence. Deferring without stating your view looks like avoidance, and the director reads it as a lack of conviction.

choices.text: Push back hard and point out that the director's last expansion lost money
choices.outcome: You win the point and lose the room. The board remembers the attack, not the evidence, and the director becomes an opponent on every later decision.

cards.title: Your 1 a.m. emails are a message
cards.body:
At this level **attention**, not time, is your scarcest resource. Audit four weeks of your calendar, hand over the decisions your managers should own, and block regular thinking time.

Then watch what you model. If you email at 1 a.m. and add 'no need to reply tonight', people still reply in minutes, because they copy what you **do**, not what you say. **Schedule late messages for the morning** and **state the team's response-time norm openly**. Stronger wording or praising non-replies still keeps night messaging at the centre.

cards.title: Base Camp take-aways
items: Leading leaders changes your skills, your use of time and what you value: your output is now your managers' capability.
Write values as specific operating principles, test them on real dilemmas and apply them the same way whoever is asking.
Emotional intelligence builds from self-awareness up; create a gap between trigger and response, because regulation is not suppression.
Repair public damage publicly, without a 'but', and change a routine so people see it will not happen again.
Power filters feedback: ask specific, forward-looking questions and reward the first honest answer.
Presence is composure, clarity and credibility: lead with the bottom line, hold your view under pressure and change it only for better evidence.

cards.prompt: Look at your calendar for the last two weeks. What share of your time went to work your managers should own? Write one decision type you will formally hand over this month, and one operating principle you want your team to be able to predict from you.

quiz.question: Bilal has just been promoted from area sales manager to national sales head of an FMCG company, leading five regional managers. Which change in how he spends his time best reflects a successful transition?
options: Joining more distributor visits so he stays close to the market
Reviewing every regional manager's weekly route plans for accuracy
Moving time to direction, coaching his managers and peer work
Personally handling key accounts so regional managers can focus on volume
quiz.explanation: Leading leaders means spending time on direction, building managers' capability and cross-functional relationships. Market visits have value, but making them his main focus, checking route plans or taking key accounts away from his managers keeps him in his old job and weakens his regional managers.

quiz.question: Which version of a value is most useful as an operating principle for a senior leader?
options: I make promotion decisions on evidence I could show to the candidates not selected
I believe in fairness and treat all team members equally at all times
Fairness is one of our core values and guides everything we do
I aim to be a fair, honest and transparent leader in every situation, whatever the pressure
quiz.explanation: An operating principle is specific enough to change a decision. Only the first option describes a concrete behaviour that can be tested. The others restate the value in general terms and would not guide a hard choice.

quiz.question: In a quarterly review, a peer challenges Farah's numbers in front of the CEO. She feels her face go hot and wants to point out the peer's own missed targets. According to this session, what is the best immediate move?
options: Answer firmly by pointing out the peer's targets so the CEO sees a balanced picture
Stay silent for the rest of the meeting and raise a complaint with HR afterwards
Agree with the challenge to avoid conflict and correct the numbers later by email
Pause, ask the peer to clarify the specific concern, then respond on the facts
quiz.explanation: Creating a gap between trigger and response, for example by asking a clarifying question, lets reasoning catch up and keeps the discussion on facts. Counter-attacking escalates the hijack, while silence or false agreement is suppression rather than regulation.

quiz.question: In the four-area model of emotional intelligence, why is self-awareness usually treated as the foundation?
options: It is the area most valued by boards when they assess senior leaders
You cannot manage emotions you have not first noticed
It can be measured more reliably than the other three areas
It is the only area that cannot be developed through coaching
quiz.explanation: The areas build on each other: noticing your own emotions makes self-management possible and frees attention to read others. The other options are not reasons given for its foundational role, and self-awareness can certainly be developed.

quiz.question: Which statement about the Johari window and seniority is most accurate?
options: The hidden area shrinks automatically as leaders gain authority
The blind area tends to grow because power filters candid feedback
The unknown area disappears once a leader completes a 360 review
The open area grows naturally as people respect a leader's position
quiz.explanation: As leaders rise, people become more cautious about telling them uncomfortable truths, so the blind area tends to grow unless the leader actively seeks feedback. The other statements are not supported: none of these changes happens automatically.

quiz.question: Usman, a new plant head in Faisalabad, asks his managers, 'Any feedback for me?' at the end of every meeting and always hears 'No, sir, all good.' What change is most likely to produce useful feedback?
options: Announce that giving upward feedback is now mandatory and will be part of appraisals
Stop asking, since the managers have clearly said things are fine
Bring in an external consultant to observe meetings for a month
Ask a specific, forward-looking question and respond without defending
quiz.explanation: Specific, forward-looking questions are easier to answer honestly, and how the leader reacts to the first candid answer decides whether more follow. Making feedback mandatory adds pressure without safety; stopping accepts the filter; an observer may help but does not open the channel with his managers.

quiz.question: Rabia, head of compliance at a bank, must brief the managing director in a five-minute slot on whether to pause a new digital account product. Which opening is strongest?
options: I recommend pausing the launch for four weeks until two KYC control gaps are closed
Let me take you through how our review unfolded over the last month
There are several issues we have found that I would like to discuss
Before I give a view, it is important that you understand the full regulatory background
quiz.explanation: Senior briefings should lead with the bottom line and the decision needed, then give reasons. Narrating the review, listing issues without a view, or starting with background risks losing the listener before the recommendation is heard.

quiz.question: After publicly snapping at a zonal manager, a regional head wants to repair the damage. Which approach best fits the guidance in this session?
options: Apologise privately and leave it there, so the incident is not reopened in front of the whole team
Say nothing, and show warmth to the manager over the following weeks instead
Apologise privately, acknowledge it publicly and change a routine to invite risks early
Apologise publicly, while explaining the pressure he was under from his director
quiz.explanation: Public damage needs a repair at least as visible as the harm, plus a structural change so people see it will not recur. A private apology alone leaves the group's lesson ('bad news is punished') in place, silence fixes nothing, and an apology padded with excuses weakens it.

quiz.question: Zainab, a newly appointed head of HR, audits her last four weeks and finds 60% of her time went on approving routine leave exceptions and resolving individual payroll queries. What should she do first?
options: Work longer hours for a few months so she can add strategic work on top of current tasks
Ask her assistant to filter her emails so she only sees urgent items
Accept it, since responsive service builds credibility with the business
Define which decisions her managers will own and redirect queries to them
quiz.explanation: The audit shows she is doing work her managers should own. Handing over decision rights frees attention for strategic people work and builds her team. Longer hours are unsustainable, email filtering does not move the decisions, and accepting the pattern keeps her in the wrong job.

quiz.question: In a board meeting, a senior director dismisses Omer's recommendation to delay an acquisition. Omer believes the due diligence is incomplete. What does executive presence look like here?
options: Withdraw the recommendation, since openly disagreeing with a senior director in a board meeting is unwise
Restate the recommendation calmly with the key evidence, and stay open to better arguments
Escalate immediately to the chairperson to overrule the director
Raise his voice slightly to show conviction and keep the floor
quiz.explanation: Presence in hierarchical settings means stating a view respectfully but clearly, holding it when pushed back on, and changing it only for a better argument, not for seniority. Withdrawing abandons a reasoned view, escalating publicly damages trust, and raising his voice replaces substance with force.

sessions.title: Strategic Thinking and Decisions Under Uncertainty
sessions.summary: Senior leaders are paid to make the calls others cannot. Learn to frame the real problem, match your decision approach to the level of uncertainty, use scenarios and expected value, catch the biases that distort judgement and make trade-offs with clear decision rights.
objectives: Describe strategy as a set of explicit choices, including what not to do
Frame a problem precisely before solving it, using issue trees and testable hypotheses
Choose a decision approach that fits clear, complicated, complex or chaotic situations
Use scenarios, expected value and reversibility to decide under uncertainty
Recognise and reduce common cognitive biases and clarify who decides

cards.title: The Bhurban offsite
cards.setting: Strategy offsite at a hill resort in Bhurban. Mist outside, a projector humming inside.

lines.text: Here it is: Ascent 2028. Grow revenue 15% a year. Become the most loved snacks brand in Pakistan. Be number one in the north. Questions?
One. Those are goals, Javed. Where is the strategy? Which markets do we enter, and what do we stop doing to pay for it?
That is what our new divisional head is for. Quetta and Peshawar: both, one, or neither? I want a recommendation in three weeks.
Last time we pushed into a new city, we cut the sales force to fund it. Distributors got fewer visits, and we lost more shelf space than we saved.
Welcome to Camp I, the Icefall. The ground looks solid and cracks underneath. You cannot see the whole route, so you must learn to decide without certainty.
The question is not 'What is the answer?' yet. It is 'What is the real question?'

cards.title: Strategy is a set of choices

scenes.heading: Goals are not strategy
scenes.narration: Grow fifteen percent. Be the most loved brand. These are hopes. A strategy is a coherent set of choices about where to compete and how to win, made with limited money and real competitors.

scenes.heading: Where will we play?
scenes.narration: Which customers, cities, products and channels will you focus on, and which will you deliberately not serve?

scenes.heading: How will we win there?
scenes.narration: Why will customers choose you over the alternatives? Cost, speed, quality, relationships? And what capabilities must you build, partner for, or buy?

scenes.heading: What will we stop?
scenes.narration: If nothing is being stopped, you have probably not made a real choice. Stopping is what frees money and attention for the choices that matter.

scenes.heading: And then what?
scenes.narration: Strategic thinkers trace second and third effects before deciding. Ask 'and then what?' at least twice, and you will catch the costs that a first glance hides.

cards.title: The cut that cost more than it saved
cards.caption: Sana's memory, as a chain. Asking 'and then what?' before deciding would have exposed it.

items.label: First effect
items.detail: Cut order bookers in interior Sindh by 30% and save PKR 60 million.

items.label: Second effect
items.detail: Retailers get fewer visits and start favouring a competitor's order booker.

items.label: Third effect
items.detail: Shelf share falls and next year's regional revenue drops by PKR 110 million.

items.label: Net result
items.detail: The saving is wiped out almost twice over.

cards.title: Goal or strategic choice?
cards.prompt: Faraz scribbles on the flipchart. Sort each line from Javed's deck and the team's notes.

items.text: Grow revenue 15% a year
Serve Peshawar retailers through a partner distributor, not our own depot
Become the most loved snacks brand
Stop selling the low-margin family pack in interior Sindh
Be number one in the north
Win small retailers with 24-hour delivery instead of deeper discounts
Become a world-class organisation
Partner for cold chain instead of building our own fleet

cards.title: Frame the problem before you solve it
cards.body:
The costliest mistake in senior decisions is solving the wrong problem well.

1. **Write a specific question.** Good framing is specific, measurable, bounded in scope and time, and does **not assume the cause**.
2. **Break it down with an issue tree:** branches that do not overlap and together cover the whole problem, split until each can be tested with data.
3. **Form a hypothesis early,** then look for evidence that would prove it **wrong**. This is faster than collecting every data set, and it guards against confirmation bias.
4. **Ask 'what would have to be true?'** for each option, then test the least certain condition first.
5. **Judge ideas, not presenters.** Agreed criteria let a junior analyst's evidence beat a senior's opinion.

cards.title: From symptom to a question you can solve
cards.caption: Each step narrows the problem without assuming why it is happening.

items.label: 'Sales are down'
items.detail: A symptom. Vague, with no scope and no time frame.

items.label: Repeat orders are falling
items.detail: Better: which part of sales is falling.

items.label: Tier-2 retailers in KP
items.detail: Bounded: who, and where.

items.label: The framed question
items.detail: Why have repeat orders from Tier-2 KP retailers fallen 18% since March, and how do we recover by December?

cards.question: Which problem statement is best framed for a senior decision?
options: How do we stop competitors stealing our customers in Peshawar?
Our sales team in the north is underperforming and needs fixing
What should we do about the north?
Why has our share of new retail outlets in Peshawar fallen from 30% to 21% this year, and how can we reach 28% by June?
cards.explanation: The last option is specific, measurable, bounded in scope and time, and does not assume a cause. The first assumes competitors are the cause, the second blames the sales team without evidence, and the third has no scope, measure or time frame.

cards.title: Three weeks of data, no answer
cards.setting: Your office, one week before the deadline. Daniyal has brought a laptop full of spreadsheets.

lines.text: We have pulled every data set we could find on Quetta: census, road freight, competitor prices, rainfall. Forty-one tabs. I still cannot tell you what to do.
That is because you never asked a question. What is your best guess about why Quetta would work, and what would prove it wrong?
My guess? Retailers will stock a Punjab brand without heavy credit. And transport stays under 6% of sales.
Good. Now you have something to test. But first, look at the terrain. Is this a problem experts can analyse to an answer, or one where nobody can know until you try?
On the icefall, using the wrong method for the ground under your feet is how expeditions fall into crevasses.

cards.title: Cynefin: match the method to the terrain
cards.caption: Dave Snowden's framework. When you do not know which domain you are in (confusion), break the problem into parts. Beware complacency: rigidly applying 'clear' rules after conditions change can tip you into chaos.

items.label: Complex: probe, sense, respond
items.detail: Cause and effect clear only in hindsight. Run small safe-to-fail experiments; amplify what works.

items.label: Complicated: sense, analyse, respond
items.detail: Knowable with expertise. Use experts to compare options against agreed criteria.

items.label: Chaotic: act, sense, respond
items.detail: Crisis with no visible pattern. Act to stabilise first, then assess.

items.label: Clear: sense, categorise, respond
items.detail: Cause and effect obvious. Apply best practice, but watch for change.

cards.title: Read the terrain
cards.prompt: Match each situation in the division to the right Cynefin approach.

pairs.left: Choosing between two proven ERP systems, with internal experts
pairs.right: Complicated: get expert analysis of both against agreed criteria, then decide

pairs.left: Turning order bookers into retail advisers; nobody has done it before
pairs.right: Complex: run several small pilots in different territories and scale what works

pairs.left: A fire stops the Gujranwala plant at night
pairs.right: Chaotic: act immediately to make people and site safe, then assess

pairs.left: Onboarding a standard new distributor
pairs.right: Clear: apply the established checklist

pairs.left: The team argues about which kind of problem this is
pairs.right: Confusion: split the problem into parts and place each part in its domain

cards.question: For eight years, the division used the same distributor credit rules with almost no defaults. After a sudden currency crash, officers kept applying the standard rules, and defaults surged within weeks. Which risk does this show?
options: Treating a chaotic crisis as complicated by over-analysing
Complacency in the clear domain, letting a changed situation tip into chaos
Running too many experiments in a complex domain
Disagreement between experts in the complicated domain
cards.explanation: Rigidly applying best practice after conditions have changed is the complacency trap of the clear domain, and it can push a situation suddenly into chaos. There is no sign of over-analysis, experiments or expert disagreement: the officers simply kept following the old rules.

cards.title: The Quetta depot, in expected value
cards.caption: Expected value = each outcome × its probability, added up: 0.6 × 50 + 0.4 × (−20) = 30 − 8 = PKR 22m. A useful anchor, but not the whole answer: can the business survive the downside?

items.label: Chance of success
items.detail: Profit of PKR 50 million in year one.

items.label: Chance of failure
items.detail: Loss of PKR 20 million.

items.label: Expected value
items.detail: Above the certain PKR 15m from expanding in southern Punjab instead.

items.label: Downside to survive
items.detail: Would it breach a loan covenant? If so, the safer option may be wiser.

cards.title: Three more tools for uncertainty
cards.body:
**Scenario planning.** Instead of one forecast, describe two to four plausible futures built on the most important and most uncertain drivers, such as inflation or the exchange rate. Prefer **robust** choices that perform acceptably in all of them, and avoid any option that risks unacceptable harm (such as a covenant breach) in one. Agree **signposts** that show which future is unfolding.

**Reversibility.** A **one-way door** (closing a plant, a ten-year exclusive contract, selling a brand) deserves careful senior analysis. A **two-way door** (a six-week price test in one city) should be decided quickly, close to the work. Central approval of two-way doors slows learning and teaches people to fear action.

**Keep options open.** When uncertainty is high, buy learning cheaply: pilots, phased investment, partnerships with exit clauses.

cards.front: Closing the old Kot Lakhpat packing line
cards.back: One-way door. Costly or impossible to undo: analyse carefully and involve senior leaders.

cards.front: A six-week price test on one product in Multan
cards.back: Two-way door. Cheap to reverse: let the people closest to the market decide quickly.

cards.front: A ten-year exclusive distributor contract with heavy exit penalties
cards.back: One-way door. The penalties lock you in, so it deserves full senior scrutiny.

cards.front: Trying a new route plan in one Faisalabad territory
cards.back: Two-way door. Decide near the work and learn fast; central approval would only slow it.
An option that performs acceptably across every plausible scenario, rather than brilliantly in one and disastrously in another.
An early indicator, agreed in advance, that tells you which scenario is starting to unfold.

cards.title: The warehouse that would not stop
cards.setting: Steering committee for the automated warehouse at Sundar Industrial Estate.

lines.text: Two years ago, before your time, the group began an automated warehouse. PKR 420 million spent. The vendor's new estimate: 14 more months and PKR 250 million more.
We have come too far to stop now. Four hundred and twenty million! We finish it.
Around the table, heads nod. Nobody looks at the vendor's slipping milestones.
I have doubts, but who argues with Javed sahib in this room?
Two traps in one room: money already spent, and a boss who speaks first. You have one chance to change how this decision is made. What do you do?

cards.title: Break the spell of sunk cost
cards.situation: You chair the next steering committee. The warehouse has cost PKR 420 million so far. Finishing needs PKR 250 million more and 14 months, and the vendor has missed every milestone. Javed has already said 'we finish it'. How do you run the meeting?

choices.text: Ask: 'If we had spent nothing yet, knowing what we know today, would we choose this plan?' Then run a pre-mortem with written answers, and commission a short independent review against criteria agreed in advance
choices.outcome: The written pre-mortem surfaces what nobody said aloud: the vendor's local team keeps leaving, and two modules have never run in Pakistan. The review recommends a phased alternative that costs less. Javed accepts it because the process was fair and the evidence was clear.

choices.text: Cancel the project immediately to stop the bleeding
choices.outcome: You escape the sunk cost but skip the analysis. Exit costs, contract penalties and a cheaper phased option were never examined. Javed overturns you within a week, and you have lost the room.

choices.text: Agree to finish. Too much has been invested to walk away
choices.outcome: That is the sunk-cost bias speaking. The PKR 420 million is gone whatever you choose. Eighteen months later the warehouse is still not live and has cost another PKR 330 million.

choices.text: Ask the vendor to present a new, more confident plan
choices.outcome: The vendor is the one party certain to say 'continue'. You have looked only for evidence that supports the current path, which is confirmation bias.

cards.title: Seven biases and their process fixes
cards.caption: You spot biases in others far more easily than in yourself. Knowing them is not enough: build the fix into the process.

items.label: Anchoring
items.left: The first number heard sets everyone's range
items.right: Build the budget from needs before showing last year's figure

items.label: Availability
items.left: A vivid recent event feels more likely than it is
items.right: Check base rates and the cost of the response

items.label: Sunk cost
items.left: Continuing because of what is already spent
items.right: Ask: would we start this today, knowing what we know?

items.label: Confirmation
items.left: Seeking evidence for what we already believe
items.right: State a hypothesis and look for evidence that disproves it

items.label: Groupthink
items.left: Everyone agrees with the most senior voice
items.right: Written views first; most junior speaks first

items.label: Overconfidence
items.left: Plans with no margin; ranges far too narrow
items.right: Pre-mortem: imagine it failed; writing why makes doubts safe to voice

items.label: Status quo
items.left: Keeping the old way because change feels risky
items.right: Agree criteria before seeing options; compare fairly

cards.title: Spot the bias
cards.prompt: Each of these happened somewhere in the group this year. Match the moment to the bias.

pairs.left: After a PKR 4m theft at one depot, a proposal to double checks at all 60 depots
pairs.right: Availability: one vivid event is outweighing years of low-loss data

pairs.left: Every marketing budget proposal lands near last year's PKR 85m
pairs.right: Anchoring: the first figure on the table is setting the range

pairs.left: 'Find me data that supports the Quetta launch'
pairs.right: Confirmation: looking only for evidence that agrees

pairs.left: Nobody disagrees with Javed until the project fails
pairs.right: Groupthink: harmony and hierarchy are suppressing dissent

pairs.left: Keeping a weak packaging vendor because switching feels risky
pairs.right: Status quo bias: preferring the current state even when change is better

cards.question: In your own reviews, your regional managers always agree with whatever you say first. You have told them, 'I want challenge,' twice, and nothing has changed. What is most likely to surface real disagreement?
options: Telling them a third time, more firmly, that you expect challenge
Collecting written views before you speak, and asking the most junior manager to speak first
Holding an open show of hands right after you give your view
Bringing in a consultant to present the counter-arguments
cards.explanation: Groupthink and anchoring on the senior voice are countered by process: independent written views and reverse-seniority speaking. Repeating the invitation has already failed, an open vote after you speak keeps the social pressure, and a consultant does not change how your managers behave.

cards.title: Who does what in a decision
cards.caption: One decider is essential. Requiring everyone to agree causes long delays and weak compromises. Keep veto rights to a few, tied to non-negotiables such as regulation and law.

items.label: Recommend
items.detail: Does the analysis and proposes an option.

items.label: Input
items.detail: Consulted for views and facts, but cannot block.

items.label: Agree
items.detail: A formal veto, e.g. compliance or legal on regulatory points only. Keep this list short.

items.label: Decide
items.detail: One named person, accountable for the call.

items.label: Carry out
items.detail: The people who make the decision work, and who commit to it.

cards.title: Disagree, then commit
cards.body:
Your recommendation goes to Javed: **pilot Peshawar through a partner distributor, postpone Quetta, and expand into southern Punjab from existing depots.** You show what you are choosing **not** to do, and why.

Faraz argued for entering Quetta as well. Javed, the named decider, listens to every input and chooses your option. That evening, Faraz's finance team asks him what he really thinks. His answer:

> 'I argued for another option. The decision is made, I am committed, and here is the reasoning.'

That is **disagree and commit**: honest about the debate, fully behind the decision, explaining the why. The opposite, 'yes in the meeting, no in the corridor', does far more damage than open disagreement beforehand. People commit more easily when they know they were genuinely heard.

cards.question: Six months later, a sudden spike in fuel prices pushes the Peshawar pilot into a loss. A board member wants to know 'who got this wrong'. What is the best response?
options: Accept the blame quickly so the board can move on
Review the quality of the reasoning and information separately from the outcome
Refuse a review, since nobody could have predicted fuel prices
Focus the review only on improving fuel-price forecasts
cards.explanation: Good decisions can have bad outcomes because of events nobody controls. Judging the reasoning separately from the result allows real learning, for example whether fuel risk was considered at all. Keeping a decision journal, noting your expectations and confidence at the time, makes this review honest. Automatic blame or no review both skip the learning, and forecasting alone is too narrow.

cards.title: Camp I take-aways
items: Strategy is explicit choices about where to play, how to win, what to build and what to stop; goals alone are not strategy.
Trace second- and third-order effects, frame the problem as a specific, unbiased question, and test hypotheses by trying to disprove them.
Match your method to the terrain: best practice when clear, experts when complicated, experiments when complex, immediate action when chaotic.
Use expected value, but check you can survive the downside; prefer robust choices, and move fast on two-way doors.
Counter biases with process: pre-mortems, criteria first, written views, reverse seniority and base rates.
Name one decider, keep vetoes few, expect disagree-and-commit, and judge decisions by their reasoning, not only their outcome.

cards.prompt: Think of a major decision on your desk right now. Which Cynefin domain is it really in, and does your approach match it? Write down what would have to be true for your preferred option to succeed, and which of those conditions you are least sure of.

quiz.question: A telecom's head of strategy presents a plan titled 'Strategy 2028' with three goals: grow revenue 15% a year, be the most loved brand and lead in 5G. What is the most important thing missing?
options: A detailed financial model showing year-by-year revenue projections
Explicit choices about where to compete, how to win and what to stop
A comparison of the plan with the strategies of global telecom operators
A communication campaign to build employee excitement about the goals
quiz.explanation: Goals are not strategy. Without choices about where to play, how to win and what not to do, the plan gives no guidance on resource allocation. A financial model, benchmarks and communication may all help, but none supplies the missing choices.

quiz.question: A pharma company cuts its medical representatives in interior Sindh by 30% to save PKR 60 million. Doctors receive fewer visits, prescriptions shift to a competitor, and next year revenue in the region falls by PKR 110 million. Which thinking habit would most likely have prevented this?
options: Benchmarking field-force size against competitors in the same region
Using expected value to calculate the most likely savings
Applying best practice from the company's Punjab operations
Tracing second- and third-order effects before deciding
quiz.explanation: The loss came from consequences beyond the first effect. Asking 'and then what?' would have exposed the link between fewer visits, lost prescriptions and lower revenue. Benchmarking and expected value of savings do not capture the chain, and copying Punjab practice ignores local conditions.

quiz.question: Which problem statement is best framed for senior decision-making?
options: Why has our share of salary accounts from new corporate clients in Karachi fallen from 22% to 15% this year, and how can we regain 20% by June?
We need to improve our performance in salary accounts across the country
Our corporate banking team is not working hard enough on new clients
Competitors are taking our customers and we must respond quickly
quiz.explanation: A well-framed problem is specific, measurable, bounded in scope and time, and does not assume the cause. The others are vague, blame a cause without evidence, or describe a reaction rather than a question.

quiz.question: A retail chain wants to change its store staff culture from 'stock keepers' to 'customer advisers'. Nobody in the company has done this before and staff reactions are hard to predict. Which approach best fits?
options: Hire a consultant to design the definitive programme, then roll it out to all stores
Apply the training programme used successfully by another retailer, unchanged
Run several small, safe-to-fail pilots in different stores and scale what works
Issue clear new standard operating procedures and audit compliance monthly
quiz.explanation: Culture change with unpredictable reactions is a complex problem, where cause and effect are clear only in hindsight. Probe-sense-respond through small experiments is the right approach. The others treat it as complicated or clear, assuming the answer can be designed or copied in advance.

quiz.question: Option A has a 70% chance of earning PKR 40 million and a 30% chance of losing PKR 30 million. Option B earns a certain PKR 15 million. What is the expected value of Option A, and what else should the leader consider?
options: PKR 19 million; whether the business could absorb a PKR 30 million loss
PKR 28 million; whether the 70% probability is reliable
PKR 10 million; whether Option B's return is truly certain
PKR 19 million; nothing else matters, since Option A clearly beats Option B on expected value
quiz.explanation: 0.7 x 40 + 0.3 x (-30) = 28 - 9 = PKR 19 million, above B's 15 million. But expected value is not the whole answer: the leader must consider the capacity to absorb the downside. The PKR 28 million figure ignores the loss, and saying nothing else matters ignores risk.

quiz.question: Which decision is best treated as a two-way door that should be made quickly and close to the work?
options: Closing the company's only plant in Hyderabad and moving production to Lahore
Signing a ten-year exclusive distribution contract with heavy exit penalties
Testing a new price point for one product in Multan for six weeks
Selling a business unit to a competitor
quiz.explanation: A limited pricing test in one city is easy and cheap to reverse, so it should be decided quickly by the people closest to it. Plant closure, long exclusive contracts with penalties and divestment are costly or impossible to undo and deserve careful senior analysis.

quiz.question: In a budget meeting, the CFO opens with, 'Last year we spent PKR 85 million on marketing.' The team's proposals all land between PKR 80 and 95 million, although the new strategy needs a very different mix. Which bias is most clearly at work, and what is the best fix?
options: Confirmation bias; ask the team to look for evidence against their proposals
Groupthink; appoint a devil's advocate for future budget meetings
Availability bias; review marketing campaigns from several years, not just the most recent one
Anchoring; build the budget from the strategy's needs before showing last year's figure
quiz.explanation: Estimates clustering around the first number heard is anchoring. The fix is to build the budget from needs before the anchor appears. The other biases may exist, but they do not explain the clustering, and their fixes would not remove the anchor.

quiz.question: Before approving a major market entry, the managing director asks the team to imagine that, one year later, it has failed badly, and to write down why. What is the main purpose of this technique?
options: To lower the team's expectations so they are not disappointed later
To make it safe to voice doubts and surface risks optimism hides
To calculate the probability of failure more precisely
To prepare the explanation the board will need if the project fails
quiz.explanation: A pre-mortem legitimises doubt and surfaces risks that people would not raise in an optimistic planning meeting. It is not about lowering expectations, does not produce precise probabilities, and is not mainly about preparing excuses.

quiz.question: A family-owned textile group has decisions stalling for months because five directors must all agree on any capital spend above PKR 10 million. What change would most improve decision speed without losing important input?
options: Name one accountable decider per decision type, keep veto rights to a few, and consult others
Raise the approval threshold to PKR 50 million so that fewer decisions need all five directors to agree
Require all five directors to meet weekly so decisions are made faster
Let the chairman override any director who has not responded within a month
quiz.explanation: Clarifying decision roles, with one decider, a short list of those who must agree, and others giving input, removes the unanimity trap while keeping input. Raising the threshold only moves the problem, weekly meetings keep unanimity, and a one-month override still allows long delays.

quiz.question: After a well-reasoned decision to enter a new segment, an unexpected currency shock causes a loss. In the review, the board wants to blame the decision-makers. What is the most appropriate leadership response?
options: Accept the blame, since a loss proves the decision was wrong
Argue that losses after careful analysis are always due to bad luck, so no review is needed
Focus the review only on finding which forecast was most wrong
Review the quality of the reasoning and information separately from the outcome
quiz.explanation: Good decisions can produce bad outcomes through events outside anyone's control. Judging reasoning separately from results allows real learning, for instance about whether currency risk was considered. Accepting blame automatically or denying any review both skip that learning, and focusing only on forecasts is too narrow.

sessions.title: Building High-Performing Teams and Leading Leaders
sessions.summary: On the high ice, every climber is roped to others. Turn a group of capable managers into a real leadership team: build trust and psychological safety, hold people accountable without blame, delegate outcomes at scale and coach leaders to grow.
objectives: Distinguish a real leadership team from a group of managers who report to the same person
Build trust and psychological safety and explain why they improve performance
Create accountability through clear commitments and follow-through, without blame
Delegate outcomes and decision rights matched to each manager's readiness
Coach leaders using structured conversations and behaviour-based feedback

cards.title: Five climbers, one rope end
cards.setting: Monday management meeting, divisional office, Lahore. Six chairs, five laptops, one tense silence.

lines.text: Every Monday, each of your five regional managers presents their own numbers for fifteen minutes, then leaves. Problems between regions come to you, one at a time, in private.
Potohar hit 104% again. But Lahore's promotions keep draining stock we were promised. I have raised it with you three times.
KP is at 78%. Two quarters in a row. The new territory is much bigger than my old area, and I do not know what to fix first.
Your managers are not accountable. Each one hits a number while the division misses its growth target. Fix it.
Welcome to Camp II. On the high ice every climber is roped to the others. Right now you have five climbers each holding a rope that ends in your hand.
Is this a leadership team, or a group of managers who happen to report to the same person?

cards.title: What makes a real leadership team

scenes.heading: Hub and spoke
scenes.narration: In a hub-and-spoke group, each manager deals only with the boss about their own area. Meetings are individual updates. Nobody owns the whole.

scenes.heading: Shared goals
scenes.narration: A real team has collective goals no member can reach alone, like on-shelf availability, which needs sales, supply and marketing together. Members truly depend on each other.

scenes.heading: Enabling structure
scenes.narration: The right size, often five to nine people. Clear norms on how you decide and disagree. And meetings built for joint problem-solving, not reporting.

scenes.heading: Supportive context
scenes.narration: Information, resources and rewards must back collective success. If every bonus depends only on individual targets, expect individual behaviour, however often you say 'team'.

scenes.heading: The first team
scenes.narration: Finally, each member must treat the peer group as their first team, putting the whole division ahead of defending their own patch. You build that with shared goals, shared rewards and by calling out turf protection.

items.label: Goals
items.right: Collective goals nobody reaches alone

items.label: Meetings
items.right: Joint work on cross-functional problems

items.label: Conflicts
items.right: Resolved between peers, openly

items.label: Rewards
items.right: A meaningful share tied to shared goals

items.label: Loyalty
items.right: This team is my first team

cards.question: You set three shared division goals, but each manager's bonus stays 100% tied to their own region. Six months later, they still protect their own areas. What change will most likely help?
options: A team-building retreat in Nathia Gali
Repeating the shared goals at every Monday meeting
Linking a meaningful share of every bonus to the shared goals
Replacing the two most territorial managers
cards.explanation: Teams need a supportive context in which rewards reinforce collective success. Individual-only bonuses predictably produce individual behaviour. Retreats and repetition leave the incentive untouched, and new managers would face the same system.

cards.title: Trust and psychological safety
cards.body:
**The trust equation** (popularised by David Maister and colleagues):

**Trust = (Credibility + Reliability + Intimacy) ÷ Self-orientation**

Because self-orientation sits **below the line**, a leader seen as focused on their own image or promotion loses trust faster than anything else can build it.

**Psychological safety** (Amy Edmondson) is a shared belief that it is safe to ask, admit a mistake, raise a concern or challenge an idea. Her hospital research found that better-led teams **reported more** medication errors: not because they made more, but because people felt safe to report them, so errors were caught and fixed.

Safety is **not** niceness or low targets. Leaders build it by framing work as learning ('this is new for all of us, so flag problems early, including with my ideas'), admitting their own mistakes and meeting bad news with thanks and action.

cards.title: Safety and standards need each other
cards.caption: The best teams combine high safety with high standards. Safety replaces fear, not effort.

items.label: Comfort zone
items.detail: High safety, low standards. Pleasant, flexible targets, flat results.

items.label: Learning and performance zone
items.detail: High safety, high standards. People stretch, speak up and fix problems early.

items.label: Apathy zone
items.detail: Low safety, low standards. People keep their heads down and do the minimum.

items.label: Anxiety zone
items.detail: Low safety, high standards. Pressure without voice: problems are hidden until they explode.

cards.title: Builds safety or erodes it?
cards.prompt: You overhear these lines across the division this week. Which build psychological safety, and which erode it?

items.text: 'This is new for all of us, so flag problems early, including with my plan.'
'Bring me solutions, not problems.'
A manager opens a review by naming her own mistake first
'Who exactly is responsible for this mess?'
'Thank you for telling me early. What do you need?'
Laughing at a junior officer's question in front of the team
Asking a genuine question, then waiting through the silence
Quietly sidelining the person who challenged the plan

cards.title: The trust equation, piece by piece

cards.back: Do you know what you are talking about, and are you honest about what you do not know?
Do you do what you say, consistently, week after week?
Do people feel safe telling you difficult or personal things?
Are you focused on yourself (your image, your promotion, winning the argument)? It is the denominator, so it damages trust most.

cards.front: The brilliant manager nobody confides in
cards.back: Always on time, technically excellent, but seen as positioning for the next job: high self-orientation is dragging his trust down.

cards.front: Why did safer hospital teams report more errors?
cards.back: People felt safe to speak up, so more mistakes were surfaced and fixed. Fewer reports can mean more hiding.

cards.title: The lease nobody approved
cards.setting: A phone call from Peshawar, Friday afternoon.

lines.text: Good news! I have signed a 12-month lease for a warehouse in Hayatabad. Within budget, within policy. You said to handle the warehousing.
Your stomach drops. You meant: find options and bring me a recommendation.
A 12-month lease in my numbers without a word to finance? Who authorised this?
Did he overstep, or did you never say where his authority ended? Most delegation fights come from two people assuming different levels.

cards.title: Five levels of delegated authority
cards.caption: Make the level explicit for every area you hand over. Daniyal thought he was at level 3; you expected level 2.

items.label: 1. Inform
items.detail: Gathers the facts; you decide.

items.label: 2. Recommend
items.detail: Proposes a decision; you approve it.

items.label: 3. Decide and tell
items.detail: Decides, then informs you.

items.label: 4. Decide
items.detail: Decides and acts; you review periodically.

items.label: 5. Full ownership
items.detail: Owns the area, including setting its goals.

cards.title: What do you do about the lease?
cards.situation: Daniyal signed a 12-month warehouse lease after you told him to 'handle the warehousing'. It is within budget and policy, and the site looks sound. You had expected to approve the choice first. Faraz is irritated. What now?

choices.text: Accept the decision because it is sound, own the unclear brief, and agree a one-page delegation note with explicit authority levels for future contracts
choices.outcome: Daniyal relaxes and asks good questions about where his limits are. Faraz agrees to the authority levels, and the next contract comes to you as a recommendation, exactly as agreed. Daniyal's initiative survives.

choices.text: Accept the lease, but tell Daniyal privately that he overstepped
choices.outcome: The lease stands, but Daniyal hears that he is to blame for an instruction you never made clear. Next time he waits for you on everything, and your queue grows again.

choices.text: Cancel the lease to show who approves contracts
choices.outcome: You pay a penalty, embarrass Daniyal in front of a landlord and teach every manager that initiative is punished. All of it caused by your unclear delegation.

choices.text: Take back all warehousing decisions for KP yourself
choices.outcome: You are the bottleneck again, on a territory 400 km away. Daniyal learns nothing, and his confidence drops just when he needs it most.

cards.title: Match the style to the readiness
cards.prompt: Readiness is task-specific: competence plus commitment for this task. Match each manager to the style that fits.

pairs.left: A confident, experienced controller running a budget process for the first time
pairs.right: Directing: clear instructions and close check-ins for this new task, despite his overall experience

pairs.left: A skilled HR partner, discouraged after two rejected proposals
pairs.right: Supporting: on a project she has done before, she needs encouragement and involvement, not instruction

pairs.left: A keen new manager with some skill who is still learning the task
pairs.right: Coaching: direction plus explanation, questions and encouragement

pairs.left: A highly skilled, motivated manager on a task she has mastered
pairs.right: Delegating: hand over the outcome and authority, and review periodically

pairs.left: A new treasury officer in a live payment failure at month-end
pairs.right: Crisis directing: no time to explore, so give clear instructions now and debrief later

cards.title: Write a one-page delegation agreement
cards.body:
For any significant area you hand over, agree on one page:

- **Outcome:** what success looks like, in measurable terms
- **Authority level:** which decisions they make alone, which they recommend
- **Boundaries:** budget, policies, anything that must be escalated
- **Support:** people, data and access you will provide
- **Check-ins:** when you will review, and what triggers an earlier talk

**Common mistake:** delegating the work but not the authority. Responsibility without power demotivates capable people fast. And remember: delegate **outcomes and decision rights**, not tasks one by one.

cards.title: The accountability loop
cards.caption: Accountability is not blame. Most 'accountability problems' start on the leader's side of this loop: changing targets, forgetting follow-ups, or applying consequences to some people but not others.

items.label: Clear expectations
items.detail: What outcome, by when, and what good looks like.

items.label: Explicit commitment
items.detail: The person agrees, ideally in their own words.

items.label: Predictable follow-through
items.detail: Progress reviewed on a rhythm everyone knows.

items.label: Consistent consequences
items.detail: Recognition when met; a direct private talk when not; the same rules for everyone.

cards.question: For the fourth quarter running, the Gujranwala regional manager misses the deadline for his board-pack section, and you stay up all night finishing it. What should you do?
options: Keep finishing it yourself; the board pack matters too much
Quietly give the section to another manager from now on
Discuss the pattern with him, hand ownership back with clear checkpoints, and stop rescuing
Refer him to HR for a formal performance process straight away
cards.explanation: Routine rescuing teaches a manager that someone else will meet his deadlines. A direct conversation, renewed ownership and agreed checkpoints restore accountability. Reassigning quietly or going straight to HR skips the conversation and leaves the cause undiagnosed. Rescuing occasionally in a real crisis is fine; doing it every quarter is not.

cards.title: Stop being the complaints channel
cards.body:
Sana keeps telling you privately that Lahore drains her stock. If you carry every complaint between managers, **peer accountability** never develops.

- Set a team norm: issues are raised **directly** with the colleague, then in the room if unresolved.
- Coach managers on how to do it ('You committed to the stock plan by Thursday; it came Monday and our launch slipped').
- In reviews after a failure, look at **both** system causes **and** which commitments were missed, and follow up consistently. Ignoring individual commitments confuses safety with low standards; hunting one scapegoat ignores the system.

cards.title: Coaching Daniyal
cards.setting: A quiet corner of a dhaba outside Mardan, after a day of market visits.

lines.text: For two quarters you have told Daniyal exactly what to do in each review. Nothing has changed. Javed wants him replaced.
Before you judge, diagnose. Strong record, much bigger and harder territory. Is it clarity, skill, will, fit, or the territory itself?
So tonight you ask instead of tell. 'What is really happening out there?'

Honestly? Visits are fine. But new retailers stop ordering after a month because our distributor gives no credit, and the competitor gives 30 days. My target counts new outlets, not active ones, so I never raised it.
Months of instructions never found that. One good question did. Now help him build his own way forward.

cards.title: The GROW coaching conversation
cards.prompt: Put the four stages of a GROW coaching conversation with Daniyal in order.
steps: Goal: 'What do you want to get out of this conversation, and this quarter?'
Reality: 'What is happening now? What have you tried, and what is getting in the way?'
Options: 'What could you do? What else? What would you do with no constraints?'
Way forward: 'What exactly will you do, by when, and how committed are you, from 1 to 10?'

cards.question: Near the end of the conversation, Daniyal says, 'I suppose I will talk to the distributor about credit at some point.' What is the best next question?
options: What exactly will you propose, by when, and how committed are you from 1 to 10?
Have you thought about escalating it to Faraz instead?
What other options could you consider?
Why have you not raised this before?
cards.explanation: 'At some point' shows the Way forward stage is not finished: firm up a specific action, a date and a commitment level. Suggesting Faraz is advice disguised as a question, asking for more options goes back a stage, and asking 'why not before' returns to Reality and invites defensiveness.

cards.title: Leading through other managers
cards.body:
- **Coach, mentor or direct?** Coaching helps capable people solve problems with better thinking; mentoring shares your experience; directing suits a crisis or a true beginner. Resist the urge to fix: ask one more question.
- **Skip-levels, done right.** Tell managers about them, listen rather than instruct, and send issues back through the manager.
- **Never reverse a manager publicly.** People learn the real authority is you and start bypassing your managers. Discuss changes privately and let the manager announce them.
- **Former peers.** Like Sana, they need the same direct, private conversations as anyone else. Favouritism and harshness to prove fairness both destroy trust.
- **Underperforming managers.** Diagnose first, then set clear expectations, support and a time frame. Moving them sideways just relocates the problem.

cards.title: The skip-level shortcut
cards.situation: On a market visit in Mardan, a senior order booker stops you in front of eight colleagues: 'Sir, Daniyal sahib's new beat roster is unfair. You are the big boss. Please change it now.' Daniyal is standing two metres away.

choices.text: Listen carefully, thank him, say you will discuss it with Daniyal, then talk to Daniyal privately and let him announce any change
choices.outcome: The order booker feels heard, and Daniyal's authority stays intact. In private, Daniyal adjusts one beat that was genuinely unfair and explains the change to his team himself. People keep coming to him, not around him.

choices.text: Overturn the roster on the spot to show you care about the frontline
choices.outcome: The team cheers. From next week, every complaint in KP skips Daniyal and lands on your phone. His authority collapses, and so does your time.

choices.text: Promise to look into it and ask HR to review the roster
choices.outcome: The issue is not lost, but you have sent it around Daniyal rather than through him. He hears about it from HR and wonders why you did not talk to him first.

choices.text: Tell the order booker to follow his manager's roster and stop complaining
choices.outcome: You protect the chain of command but shut down a frontline voice. The complaint goes underground, and the next problem reaches you only when it is a crisis.

cards.title: Feedback: situation, behaviour, impact
cards.body:
Describe the **situation** (when and where), the **behaviour** (what a camera would record) and the **impact** (on people or results). Then ask for their view.

'In Tuesday's distributor meeting (situation), you shared draft prices before they were approved (behaviour). The distributor now expects that rate (impact). What was your thinking?'

**Common mistake:** labels such as 'You were careless' or hearsay such as 'People say you...'. Labels invite defence; descriptions invite discussion.

cards.title: Camp II take-aways
items: A real leadership team has shared goals, interdependence, clear norms and rewards that back collective success; hub-and-spoke is not a team.
Trust rises with credibility, reliability and intimacy, and falls sharply with self-orientation.
Combine high psychological safety with high standards; safety means people speak up, not that the bar drops.
Accountability needs clear expectations, commitment, follow-through and consistent consequences; stop rescuing and build peer accountability.
Delegate outcomes with an explicit authority level, matched to each person's readiness for that specific task.
Diagnose before judging, coach with GROW, give SBI feedback and route skip-level issues back through your managers.

cards.prompt: Is your management team a real team or a hub and spoke? Name one shared goal that would make your managers depend on each other, and one place where you are still rescuing a manager instead of holding them accountable.

quiz.question: A head of operations runs a weekly meeting where each of six managers presents their own numbers and then leaves. Cross-functional problems are solved one-to-one with the head. What best describes this group?
options: A high-performing team that uses meeting time efficiently and avoids unnecessary debate
A self-managing team with strong peer accountability
A real team that simply needs shorter meetings
A hub-and-spoke group rather than a real leadership team
quiz.explanation: When members deal only with the leader and meetings are individual updates, there is no shared ownership or interdependence. It is a hub-and-spoke group. Efficiency, self-management or meeting length are not the issue; the missing element is collective work.

quiz.question: Edmondson's research found that better-led hospital teams reported more medication errors. What is the best explanation?
options: Better-led teams took on more complex and critically ill patients, so they made more errors
People felt safer to report mistakes, so more errors were surfaced and fixed
Better-led teams were stricter and punished errors more often
Weaker teams had better systems that prevented errors
