A capable regional head is unsure how to win over a sceptical distributor
A team leader is deciding how to restructure his own shift rosters
bank.explanation: Directing suits a crisis, especially with someone new to the task, where there is no time to explore. The other situations involve capable people with problems they can solve with better thinking, which is where coaching adds most value.

bank.question: Shazia, an area manager with a strong five-year record, has missed targets for two quarters since taking over a larger territory that includes Gilgit-Baltistan. Her regional head is under pressure to act. What should he do first?
options: Start a formal performance improvement plan to show the board he is acting
Diagnose whether the cause is clarity, skill, motivation or the new territory itself
Move her back to her old territory, where she succeeded, and appoint someone else to the larger one
Wait another quarter, since strong performers usually recover on their own
bank.explanation: Diagnosis comes first: a strong record plus a much larger, harder territory suggests circumstances or new skill gaps rather than will. A formal plan before diagnosis may be unfair, moving her sideways relocates the problem without understanding it, and waiting delays help.

bank.question: Members of a GM's leadership team regularly come to her privately to complain about each other's missed commitments. None raise it with the colleague directly. What is the most effective response?
options: Investigate each complaint and take action against the colleague concerned
Raise every complaint herself in the next team meeting, naming those involved so the issues are aired openly
Ask HR to run a team conflict-resolution workshop
Set a team norm of raising issues directly and coach members to do so, rather than acting as the channel
bank.explanation: Mature teams practise peer accountability. By acting as the go-between, the GM keeps it from developing. Investigating every complaint or airing them publicly makes her the enforcer, and a workshop may help but does not change her role as the channel.

bank.question: A product launch failed after marketing and supply each missed agreed handover dates. The CEO wants to know 'whose fault it was'. Which review approach best reflects accountability without blame?
options: Review facts and system causes, and also which commitments were missed, with consistent follow-up
Focus only on process failures, since naming individuals' missed commitments would damage psychological safety
Identify the single person most responsible and apply a visible consequence
Skip the review and focus energy on the next launch
bank.explanation: Accountability without blame looks at both the system and individual commitments, and responds consistently. Ignoring individual commitments confuses safety with low standards, scapegoating one person ignores system causes, and skipping the review loses the learning.

bank.question: Branch staff at a bank are facing a new core system, new products and a branch restructuring in the same quarter. Absenteeism is rising and staff appear overwhelmed rather than complacent. According to adaptive leadership, what should the leader do?
options: Raise urgency further by sharing more data on competitive threats
Speed up all three changes so the disruption ends sooner
Leave staff to adapt on their own, since giving the work back is key
Lower the heat: sequence the changes, add structure and give clear support
bank.explanation: Leaders regulate the heat: raising it when people are complacent, lowering it when they are overwhelmed. Here the heat is too high. More urgency or speed adds pressure, and giving the work back does not mean leaving people without structure or support.

bank.question: The sponsor of a nationwide branch transformation forms a guiding coalition of five head-office managers who have always supported him. What change would most strengthen the coalition?
options: Add more head-office managers to increase the coalition's size
Replace the coalition with an external consulting team
Add credible regional leaders, including a respected sceptic of the plan
Keep the coalition as it is, since loyalty ensures it moves fast
bank.explanation: A guiding coalition needs enough authority, credibility and expertise across the affected organisation. Respected regional leaders, including a sceptic, bring credibility and insight. More head-office loyalists add size, not credibility; consultants cannot provide internal credibility; and loyalty alone risks blind spots.

bank.question: You have limited time before a digital lending decision. Director A has high power and is currently neutral. Manager B has low power and is a vocal opponent. Director C has high power and already supports you. Where should you invest most effort first?
options: Manager B, since vocal opposition can spread quickly and turn neutral colleagues against the proposal
Director A, since moving a powerful neutral party has the largest effect on the outcome
Director C, to make sure existing support does not weaken
Equally across all three, to be seen as fair
bank.explanation: The biggest gap between current and needed stance, weighted by power, is with Director A. Manager B deserves attention and listening but has less effect on the decision; Director C needs maintaining, not most of your effort; and equal effort ignores where the decision will be won.

bank.question: In a family-owned textile group, a professional CEO plans to close an old spinning unit. The founder's eldest son has no formal role in the group but is consulted by the founder on every major decision. How should the CEO treat him?
options: As a hidden, high-power stakeholder to engage early and respectfully
As outside the decision, since he holds no formal role
As a low-power stakeholder to keep informed through the newsletter
As a blocker to be bypassed by taking the decision straight to the board
bank.explanation: Informal power in family businesses can outweigh formal titles. His influence over the founder makes him a hidden, high-power stakeholder who should be engaged early. Ignoring him, treating him as low power or bypassing him risks a late, decisive block.

bank.question: During a merger of two insurance companies, staff keep saying, 'Nobody is telling us anything; we hear more from WhatsApp groups than from management.' Final decisions on roles are still eight weeks away. What is the best response?
options: Wait until role decisions are final, so that nothing communicated now has to be corrected or withdrawn later
Ask managers to tell staff not to believe rumours on WhatsApp
Share what is known, what is not, and when each decision will be made, then update regularly
Reassure staff that no jobs will be affected so that anxiety falls
bank.explanation: This resistance comes from uncertainty. Honest, regular updates on what is known, what is not and when decisions will come reduce the vacuum rumours fill. Waiting feeds rumours, telling people not to believe them does nothing, and promising no job losses before decisions are made risks broken trust.

bank.question: You need the head of IT, who reports to the CFO, to prioritise your project. You learn he values predictability and is frustrated by business units sending vague, changing requests. Which offer is most likely to win his support?
options: A personal thank-you note to the CEO praising his team's contribution once the project is successfully delivered
A single point of contact, fixed requirements signed off upfront and agreed change control
Using your budget to pay for his team's overtime during the project
Asking the CFO to direct him to prioritise your project
bank.explanation: Influence works by offering currencies the other person values; here, reduced hassle and predictability. Recognition and money may appeal to some, but they do not address his main frustration, and going over his head to the CFO uses authority rather than influence.

bank.question: In a planning meeting, a change leader asks each regional head to state, in front of peers, the target they themselves believe their region can reach, and records it. Which persuasion principle is she mainly using?
options: Scarcity
Reciprocity
Authority
Commitment and consistency
bank.explanation: People tend to act in line with commitments they have made, especially public and self-chosen ones. This is commitment and consistency, used ethically because the targets are their own. There is no limited resource (scarcity), returned favour (reciprocity) or appeal to expertise (authority).

bank.question: A hospital group is moving to electronic patient records. Which first 'short-term win' is best chosen to build momentum?
options: One hospital cuts outpatient waiting time with digital appointments within three months
Signing the software contract with a reputable vendor and announcing it widely to all staff
Holding a launch ceremony for the transformation programme
Completing a two-year data migration ahead of schedule
bank.explanation: A good short-term win is visible, unambiguous, clearly linked to the change and achieved within months. Signing contracts and launch ceremonies are activities, not results, and a two-year migration is too far away to build early belief.

bank.question: A bank is implementing a new core banking system. Which element of the programme is the clearest adaptive challenge?
options: Migrating customer data from the legacy system accurately
Getting branches to stop using informal approvals and manual workarounds they rely on
Configuring the product parameters in the new system
Building interfaces between the core system and mobile banking
bank.explanation: Abandoning long-standing informal habits requires people to change behaviour and beliefs, an adaptive challenge. Data migration, configuration and interfaces are technical problems that experts can solve with known methods, however difficult.

bank.question: Before a board vote on outsourcing payroll, the HR director pre-briefs every director except Dr. Amina, a known sceptic, planning to 'let the numbers speak' in the meeting so she is outvoted. Which assessment is most accurate?
options: It is acceptable, because pre-briefing is a legitimate influence practice
It is acceptable as long as the data shared with all directors, including at the meeting, is accurate
It crosses into unethical politics; he should brief Dr. Amina and hear her concerns too
It is unethical only if Dr. Amina later complains to the chairman
bank.explanation: Pre-briefing is legitimate, but deliberately excluding a sceptic to win by ambush fails the transparency test and loses valuable input. Accurate data does not fix the selective process, and ethics do not depend on whether someone complains.

bank.question: A CEO has launched 'respect' as a core value. Which single action is most likely to convince staff the value is real?
options: Including the value in every town hall speech for a year
Running respect workshops for all managers
Adding the value to performance appraisal forms
Withholding promotion from a top-performing manager who mistreats staff, and explaining why
bank.explanation: Promotion decisions are among the strongest culture signals, especially when they cost something. Acting on a top performer shows the value outranks results achieved disrespectfully. Speeches, workshops and forms matter less unless real decisions back them.

bank.question: Uzma, head of finance, says, 'Our corporate culture is fear-based, so there is nothing I can do about how my team behaves.' Which response is best supported by this course?
options: She is right; culture is set by the CEO and the board and cannot really vary within individual functions
She can still shape her function's subculture through her attention, rewards and example
She should wait for a corporate culture programme before acting
She should move to another company with a better culture
bank.explanation: Large organisations contain subcultures, and a function's culture is shaped strongly by its leader's daily behaviour. The corporate culture limits but does not remove her influence. Waiting or leaving ignores what she can do now.

bank.question: A consumer finance company's executive committee discusses 'improving collections efficiency' by calling overdue borrowers' relatives and employers. The discussion is entirely about recovery rates and cost. Which leadership practice best counters ethical fading here?
options: Explicitly asking who could be harmed and how, and whether this is lawful and fair
Asking the collections team to prepare a more detailed cost-benefit analysis, including complaint-handling costs
Benchmarking the practice against what competitors do
Approving a pilot so the recovery effect can be measured
bank.explanation: Ethical fading happens when decisions are framed purely in business terms. Deliberately raising the ethical and legal question brings it back into view. More analysis, benchmarks or pilots keep the framing purely commercial, and 'others do it' is a classic rationalisation.

bank.question: A concern about expense fraud is raised through a pharma company's confidential hotline. The regional manager accused correctly guesses who reported it and tells the director he wants that employee transferred. What should the director do?
options: Transfer the employee to reduce tension while the case is investigated
Let the regional manager handle the matter within his own team
Ask the employee to withdraw the report to protect team harmony
Protect the employee from any retaliation and ensure an independent investigation
bank.explanation: People who raise concerns in good faith must be protected, and the investigation must be independent of the accused. Transferring the reporter is retaliation even if presented as reducing tension, and letting the accused handle it or seeking withdrawal destroys trust in the speak-up system.

bank.question: Saima tells a senior manager that his quarterly report contained two significant errors. He responds heatedly, 'So after 18 years you are saying I am incompetent?' Which part of the difficult conversation has surfaced, and what is the best response?
options: The 'what happened' conversation; re-explain the errors with more evidence
The feelings conversation; suggest postponing until he calms down
The identity conversation; acknowledge his record and separate this issue from his overall worth
None of them; his reaction is unprofessional and should be addressed separately as a conduct issue
bank.explanation: His reaction is about how he sees himself, the identity layer, which drives the strongest responses. Acknowledging his record while keeping the specific issue clear addresses it. More evidence ignores the real concern, postponing avoids it, and treating it as misconduct escalates the situation.

bank.question: An audit firm's Karachi office has had six months of 70-hour weeks. Staff surveys show exhaustion and cynicism, and two managers have resigned. HR proposes a monthly wellness webinar. What should the office head do?
options: Approve the webinar, as resilience training for individuals is the main solution to burnout in audit firms
Address workload, give teams more control over scheduling and plan recovery after peaks
Offer a one-time bonus to compensate for the long hours
Remind staff that long hours are normal in audit during busy season
bank.explanation: Burnout is driven mainly by working conditions such as workload and lack of control, so leaders must change those. A webinar or bonus may be welcome, but neither touches the cause, and normalising the hours deepens cynicism.

bank.question: In a talent review, HR notices that each manager has rated as 'high potential' mainly people who share their own background and style. What is the most effective remedy?
options: Hold a calibration session where managers justify ratings with evidence against shared criteria
Let HR assign potential ratings without manager input
Drop the potential dimension and rate performance only
Ask each manager to rate at least one person from a different background as high potential to balance the pool
bank.explanation: Calibration across managers against shared criteria and evidence reduces bias, including affinity for people like ourselves. Removing managers' input loses knowledge, dropping potential abandons succession planning, and quotas replace one bias with another.

bank.question: Naveed is the strongest candidate to succeed the head of sales. He has led large teams well but has never managed a profit and loss account, which the role requires. How should he be classified and developed?
options: Ready now; give him the role and let him learn P&L on the job
Ready in three or more years; enrol him in a long part-time finance degree before considering him
Ready in one to two years; give him real P&L responsibility, such as an acting role, with coaching
Not a successor; look for an external candidate with P&L experience
bank.explanation: One significant, closable gap places him in the one-to-two-year group, and challenging experience with coaching is the fastest route. Calling him ready now ignores a core requirement, a long degree is slow and indirect, and ruling him out wastes a strong internal candidate.

bank.question: A regional director avoids developing a successor because he fears being replaced. His CEO is considering him for a national role. Which statement best reflects how this is likely to be seen?
options: The CEO will value him more, since the region depends on him
It will not matter, since promotion depends only on regional results
It is wise, because a strong successor could be promoted over him
It may block his promotion, because moving him would leave a gap nobody can fill
bank.explanation: Leaders who build strong benches are seen as ready for larger roles; without a successor, moving him creates key-person risk for the region. Dependence on him is a weakness, not an asset, and results alone rarely decide promotions to wider roles.

bank.question: A plant head strictly enforces a new punctuality rule for all supervisors, but excuses his nephew, a shift supervisor, who regularly arrives late. What is the most likely effect on the plant's culture?
options: The single exception undermines the rule and signals that relationships outweigh standards
Little effect, because one exception among many supervisors is unlikely to be noticed by the workforce
A positive effect, since staff respect leaders who protect family
The rule will still work, because most supervisors are complying
bank.explanation: Consistency matters more than intensity, and one visible exception for a relative can undo the rule and teach that relationships matter more than standards. Such exceptions are almost always noticed, and current compliance is likely to fall once people see the double standard.
